text.p: In overnight commodity markets, copper closed down a touch in London while aluminium bounced back US$14 a tonne from its selloff on Tuesday.

Oil prices edged down as fundamentally strong supplies overpowered speculative buying, while gold prices ended down as uncertainty over the dispute between the German government and the Bundesbank was resolved and the U.S dollar rose.
Wheat prices hit a three month low, hit by losses in soybeans and strong harvest figures through from the U.S. plains.
The CRB index ended down 1.44 points at 247.00 in the U.S.
Base metal prices recovered from midsession their nadir during Wednesday afternoon LME trading mostly on shortcovering but a mixed close tended to favour the downside, traders said.
Copper was little changed, aluminium was firmer and the rest of the complex was comfortably above the lows but the rallies were little more than customary position squaring, they said.

By the close three months prices were little changed after recovering from a dip under $2,470, but spreads appear to be unravelling and there is little physical interest, so levels near $2,500 will be difficult to sustain at present, traders said. Last business was at $2,478 a tonne, down just $1 from Tuesday's kerb close. The cash/threes backwardation was at $52/62.
Aluminium was steadier throughout the trading day, as the market had been caught short by the sell-off on Tuesday.
However, the bounce did not recapture $1,600, and as physical availability is ample despite falling stocks, prices are seen heading lower in the short term. The market closed at $1,592, up $14.
Nickel staged an impressive rally during late trade, bolstered by the possibility of a long strike at Inco's Sudbury facilities, according to union sources.

Zinc built on earlier trade buying that emerged on dips towards $1,330 and chased higher during late afternoon ring and kerb trading. Trends in copper assisted the tone and last trade was at $1,350, up $16.

NYMEX crude oil futures prices ended mostly lower, while refined products settled lower across the board, as the market's fundamentals began to gain the upper hand on recent speculative, technical dealings. Crude oil for July delivery on the New York Mercantile Exchange lost 21 cents to end at $20.12 a barrel after trading between $20.38 and $20.08. Despite consistently ample crude supply, steady foreign imports and weakening cash-market differentials, commodity funds in the past month have coerced the market into areas that many traders said it never belonged. Inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) released Tuesday, and from the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) on Wednesday, showed rising inventories in crude, distillates and unleaded gasoline, even though refinery capacity utilization maintained a torrid production pace in the past week.

CBOT wheat futures fell to three-month lows on Wednesday, hit by limit losses in soybeans and by harvest progress in the U.S. Plains, traders said. Soybeans tumbled the 30-cent per bushel limit, hammered by news Cargill Inc was importing Brazilian soybeans for use in southeastern U.S. processing plants. Harvest progress in Texas was also cited as a bearish factor. Combines were in the fields as far north as Fort Worth, Texas. Wheat ended 8-1/4 to 4-1/4 cents per bushel lower with July down 8-1/4 at $3.53-3/4.

Gold prices ended lower in New York after the market came under pressure from a firming dollar. The June gold contract closed at US$340.90 an ounce, down US$2.10 on Tuesday's New York closing price. Traders said palladium's sharp rises had taken the market's interest.
